attacks_proposed.argument: Westport has not established the statutory delivery element as a matter of undisputed fact. The brief infers that the policies were not “issued for delivery” in Ohio from Westport’s Kansas location, PS Management’s Pennsylvania address, and the listed vehicles’ garaging locations. Those facts do not themselves establish where the policies were delivered or intended for delivery, particularly when the brief acknowledges that PS Management operated an Ohio location. As the summary-judgment movant, Westport had to point to evidence affirmatively negating the claim, with doubts construed against it; a conclusory inference about delivery is insufficient. [15]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Failure to conclusively establish out-of-state delivery defeats Westport’s primary basis for holding R.C. 3937.18 categorically inapplicable at summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: The declarations described in the brief establish listed garaging locations, but the brief does not identify evidence establishing where the vehicles were registered. More importantly, the Commercial Excess Policy identifies no vehicles at all. Westport therefore cannot simply transfer the Business Auto Policy’s vehicle schedule to the excess policy without producing and analyzing the excess policy provisions that allegedly limit all excess and retained-limit coverage to those scheduled autos. Summary judgment requires evidence affirmatively establishing the absence of a material factual issue, not an unsupported coverage inference. [15]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The statutory inapplicability argument may remain viable for the scheduled Business Auto coverage but fail as to the separately worded excess policy.

attacks_proposed.argument: Westport conflates statutory permission to incorporate a change with proof that the change was actually incorporated. The statutory language quoted in the brief says an insurer may incorporate permitted or required changes at the beginning of a policy period; it does not say every intervening amendment automatically becomes part of every renewal. The cases quoted by Westport likewise refer to a policy “actually renewed as defined in the contract.” Yet the brief does not identify the contract’s renewal definition, an endorsement adopting Senate Bill 97, or other policy language demonstrating actual incorporation on January 1, 2002. Westport bears that evidentiary burden as the summary-judgment movant. [15]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without proof of actual incorporation, Westport cannot obtain judgment on the premise that Senate Bill 97 necessarily governed the renewed policy.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief acknowledges that this Court had held in Storer that a policy cannot be amended to reflect statutory changes arising during the two-year guarantee period, and further acknowledges that the precise issue was then the subject of a certified conflict awaiting resolution by the Ohio Supreme Court. Westport’s proposed distinction rests on the timing of Senate Bill 267, but the brief does not show from the operative policy or binder that the statutory incorporation mechanism was contractually adopted. On this presentation, Westport has not established that this Court’s contrary precedent is inapplicable as a matter of law.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If Storer controls, Senate Bill 97 could not be used to eliminate coverage during the two-year period commencing December 1, 2000, defeating Westport’s alternative ground for affirmance.

attacks_proposed.argument: Westport cannot shift its summary-judgment burden by emphasizing that plaintiffs supplied no authority making nonproduction itself create UM/UIM coverage. Plaintiffs’ point also challenges whether Westport proved the terms and legal status of the coverage first bound on December 1, 2000. Because Westport relies on that inception date to define the two-year guarantee period and to establish incorporation of Senate Bill 267, Westport had to produce competent evidence of the binder’s terms and their relationship to the later policies. A statement that no physical policy was printed does not, standing alone, establish those terms. [15]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the original binder’s terms and relationship to the renewals are not established, Westport cannot prove the chronology necessary for its Senate Bill 97 theory on summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: The premise that the underlying Auto Policy contains no UM/UIM coverage conflicts with Westport’s own description of that policy. The brief states that the Business Auto Policy provides $50,000 in UM/UIM coverage for owned autos and includes Pennsylvania and Florida UM/UIM forms. Thus, the asserted absence of all underlying UM/UIM coverage is incorrect on Westport’s own account. Whether Press qualifies for that coverage is a separate policy-interpretation question that the categorical statement in this unit does not resolve.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The excess-policy argument cannot rest on the asserted complete absence of underlying UM/UIM coverage when Westport concedes that such coverage exists in at least some circumstances.

attacks_proposed.argument: Westport’s description of the Commercial Excess Policy does not establish that excess coverage exists only when the primary policy affords the same coverage. The brief states that the excess policy pays both sums above primary insurance and sums above a retained limit for certain injuries for which primary insurance is not afforded. That retained-limit feature undermines the categorical inference that the absence of underlying coverage necessarily eliminates any excess-layer obligation. Westport needed to analyze the excess policy’s insuring agreement, definitions, exclusions, and retained-limit provisions rather than rely solely on the underlying policy. [15]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: A potentially independent retained-limit obligation remains unresolved, so summary judgment on the excess policy cannot be sustained merely because Westport disputes coverage under the primary policy.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the strongest legal attack on the Senate Bill 97 alternative. The brief concedes that Storer was contrary Eighth District authority and that the precise question had been certified to the Ohio Supreme Court. A panel could not simply prefer contrary decisions from other districts. Westport does, however, directly distinguish Storer on the ground that Senate Bill 267 was already effective when this two-year period began, and it cites Arn, Advent, and St. Clair for that distinction. The attack overreaches by insisting that the policy contract itself had to adopt the statutory incorporation mechanism; the brief treats that mechanism as supplied by statute. If the Storer distinction fails, Westport loses its Senate Bill 97 ground, but not its independent argument that R.C. 3937.18 never applied.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief expressly acknowledges Storer, distinguishes it because Senate Bill 267 predated the December 2000 inception, cites contrary appellate authority, notes Shay, and discloses the pending certified conflict.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The controlling Ohio Supreme Court disposition of the Advent-Storer certified conflict, together with the complete Storer opinion, would settle the governing-law issue.

judge_assessments.assessment: This exposes a genuine gap in the standalone excess-policy analysis. The brief itself says the excess policy can pay above a retained limit for certain injuries for which primary insurance is not afforded. That language prevents the court from assuming, merely from the absence of applicable primary UM/UIM coverage, that the excess policy can never respond. The brief says the excess policy follows the automobile policy's terms, but it does not quote or analyze the provisions reconciling that follow-form language with retained-limit coverage. Generic summary-judgment authority in source 15 adds little, but the defect appears from the brief's own description. Westport could still prevail under the separate statutory-delivery ground or through the full policy language; standing alone, however, u19 is inadequately supported.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that the excess policy follows the underlying automobile policy's terms and identifies that policy as primary insurance, but it also states that the excess policy covers some injuries above a retained limit when primary insurance is not afforded. It does not reconcile those provisions.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complete excess-policy insuring agreement, retained-limit provisions, automobile follow-form clause, definitions, and exclusions are necessary to determine whether any independent coverage could exist.

judge_assessments.assessment: The registration point does not land: R.C. 3937.18 uses the alternative formulation registered or principally garaged, and the declarations allegedly establish that every scheduled auto was principally garaged in Florida or Pennsylvania. Westport therefore did not also need separate registration evidence for those autos. The attack has more force as to the excess policy because that policy lists no vehicles and the brief reaches its conclusion by importing the auto policy's schedule through an unquoted follow-form provision. Westport identifies the underlying policy and asserts that the excess policy shares its terms and limitations, which is an answer, but the record excerpts supplied here do not permit verification. The advocate risks losing only the excess-policy portion of this rationale, not necessarily the Business Auto Policy or the judgment as a whole.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief identifies all scheduled autos and their non-Ohio garaging locations, states that the excess policy is subject to the same terms, conditions, exclusions, definitions, and limitations as the identified primary auto policy, and concludes that the excess automobile coverage is confined to those autos.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review of Exhibits 3 and 5, especially the excess policy's follow-form and retained-limit provisions, would determine whether the vehicle schedule properly carries into the excess layer.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack correctly identifies imprecise wording. Westport says there is no UM/UIM coverage under the underlying policies, yet elsewhere admits that the Business Auto Policy contains $50,000 of Pennsylvania and Florida UM/UIM coverage for owned autos. The better formulation is that there is no underlying UM/UIM coverage applicable to Press's accident: he was driving his own vehicle, not a scheduled owned auto, and the admitted endorsements concern Pennsylvania and Florida risks. Thus the inconsistency weakens u19's categorical premise but does not itself establish coverage for Press. The advocate risks credibility and may be forced into a policy-specific eligibility analysis, but the point is unlikely to defeat the separate R.C. 3937.18 threshold ground.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief admits $50,000 in UM/UIM coverage for owned autos under Pennsylvania and Florida forms, while also stating that Press drove his own vehicle and was not operating any covered vehicle.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The underlying UM/UIM endorsements and the excess policy's definition of covered automobile claims would show whether the admitted coverage could conceivably apply to Press.

judge_assessments.assessment: Source 15 supports only the general summary-judgment burden; it does not establish that an out-of-state named-insured address and policy declarations are legally insufficient evidence of delivery. The brief does more than identify Westport's Kansas location: it states that review of the policies shows issuance and delivery to PS Management in Pennsylvania and cites the policies themselves. More importantly, the statutory test also concerns vehicles registered or principally garaged in Ohio, and the brief identifies every scheduled auto as garaged in Florida or Pennsylvania. The existence of an Ohio business location and an Ohio employee driving his own uncovered vehicle does not create an Ohio covered vehicle. Even if delivery evidence were debatable, this attack does not answer the independent vehicle nexus.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says the policies were issued and delivered to PS Management in Volant, Pennsylvania; cites the policies; identifies every covered auto and its Florida or Pennsylvania garaging location; and notes that Press's personal vehicle was not covered.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The declarations, mailing or delivery records, broker evidence, and affidavits in the summary-judgment record would conclusively establish the place of delivery.

judge_assessments.assessment: This largely misreads Westport's theory and the quoted authority. The brief relies on Senate Bill 267 as statutory permission to apply intervening statutory changes when an existing policy is actually renewed; it does not claim that an endorsement reciting Senate Bill 97 was required. The brief identifies a printed January 1, 2002 renewal policy, and the cited cases are presented as holding that the law effective on an actual renewal governs. Source 15 supplies only a generic burden rule and no authority for the proposed endorsement requirement. The genuine legal issue is whether Storer or the contrary renewal cases controlled, addressed in a4, not whether the policy expressly incorporated the statute.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that the policy actually renewed on January 1, 2002, cites the renewal policy and interrogatory answers, quotes the statutory incorporation provision, and cites cases holding that intervening law may govern at renewal.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full renewal provisions and controlling Ohio Supreme Court decision on the certified conflict would confirm whether actual renewal alone was sufficient.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief does not rely merely on the assertion that no physical policy was printed. It says the binder was produced and cites interrogatory answers, a compliance notice, and an affidavit establishing that coverage was bound on December 1, 2000 and renewed thereafter. That evidence, if properly in the Rule 56 record, supports the chronology without requiring a nonexistent printed policy. The attack identifies no particular binder term material to the inception date, and its demand for proof that Senate Bill 267 was contractually adopted repeats the flawed premise in a3. Plaintiffs' unsupported claim that nonproduction itself creates UM/UIM coverage remains unanswered by any authority. Westport would face a problem only if the cited exhibits failed to establish the dates or continuity asserted.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says no physical December 2000 policy existed, the binder was produced, later policies were produced, and an affidavit and interrogatory answers establish the original binding and renewal dates. It also argues that plaintiffs cited no law making nonproduction create coverage.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Inspection of the binder, affidavit, interrogatory answers, and notice of compliance would determine whether the chronology and continuity were established through admissible summary-judgment evidence.

results.assessment: The brief is strongest on the statutory-delivery and garage-location threshold, and the Storer distinction is workable enough to preserve the Senate Bill 97 theory. Its weakest points are the excess-policy analysis, where it relies on a broad follow-form assumption without fully reconciling the retained-limit language, and the categorical claim that there is no underlying UM/UIM coverage, which is overstated on the brief’s own description. The most important fix is to tighten the policy-specific explanation for why the excess form does not expand coverage and to state the underlying-coverage point more precisely. The research did not settle whether the full excess-policy language independently defeats coverage.

target.excerpt: B. SUMMARY JUDGMENT WAS PROPERLY GRANTED IN FAVOR OF APPELLEE WHERE SENATE BILL 97 GOVERNS THE WESTPORT POLICIES AND UM/UIM COVERAGE CAN NO LONGER BE IMPLIED AS A MATTER OF LAW.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands as a substantial challenge to Westport's S.B. 97 alternative. Storer was precedent from this Court and stated a rule facially adverse to mid-guarantee-period incorporation. Decisions from other districts did not displace it, and the certified conflict confirms that the issue was unsettled rather than resolved in Westport's favor. Westport does offer a material distinction—S.B. 267 was effective before this guarantee period began—but whether that distinction avoids Storer is the disputed legal question. If the Court rejects the distinction, Westport loses the S.B. 97 ground, though it may still prevail on the independent territorial ground under R.C. 3937.18.
challenges.suggested_response: Storer is distinguishable because it addressed a statutory change occurring during a two-year guarantee period that had already begun before the amendment at issue. Here, by contrast, S.B. 267 was already in effect before the Westport policies were first written on December 1, 2000, and S.B. 97 became effective on October 31, 2001, before the January 1, 2002 renewal. Under Arn, Advent, and St. Clair, the law in effect at the time of renewal governs the scope of UM/UIM coverage, and at the January 1, 2002 renewal Westport was not required to offer or include UM/UIM coverage, nor could such coverage be implied by operation of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the S.B. 97 argument, but recast it as a distinction from Storer rather than a claim that Storer has been displaced. The brief should emphasize the dates already in the record: S.B. 267 was in effect before the December 1, 2000 policy period began, and S.B. 97 became effective before the January 1, 2002 renewal.

challenges.opponent_argument: The assertion that the excess policy necessarily provides nothing unless an underlying policy provides UM/UIM coverage conflicts with Westport's own description of the excess policy. The brief states that the policy covers both sums above primary insurance and sums above a retained limit for certain injuries for which primary insurance is not afforded. That second coverage route defeats the claimed categorical dependency on underlying coverage, absent policy language specifically excluding the asserted automobile or UM/UIM risk.
challenges.why_it_matters: Westport cannot obtain summary judgment on the excess policy simply by proving that the primary policies lack UM/UIM coverage; it must also negate coverage above the retained limit under the excess policy's own terms.

challenges.judge_assessment: This exposes a real gap in the categorical excess-policy argument. Westport describes the excess policy as covering not only amounts above primary insurance but also certain injuries above a retained limit when primary insurance is unavailable. On that description alone, absence of UM/UIM coverage in the underlying policies does not necessarily eliminate every route to excess coverage. Westport must rely on the excess policy's complete insuring agreement, definitions, exclusions, and follow-form provisions to show that the retained-limit feature does not reach the claimed automobile loss. Without that showing, the dependency rationale in u19 is insufficient. Westport could still prevail on the territorial or S.B. 97 grounds if either independently applies to the excess policy.
challenges.suggested_response: The Commercial Excess Policy does not itself establish UM/UIM coverage merely because the underlying policies do not provide it. The record describes the excess policy as providing sums in excess of primary insurance and, for certain injuries, sums above a retained limit where primary insurance is not afforded; nothing in the record identifies any insuring agreement in that policy granting UM/UIM coverage independent of the underlying forms. Accordingly, on the materials before the Court, the Commercial Excess Policy does not create a genuine issue of material fact, and summary judgment in Westport's favor was proper.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the excess-policy point to what the record actually shows and stop making a categorical dependency argument. The brief should say the excess policy is described as excess liability coverage and that the record identifies no independent UM/UIM grant in that policy; if the actual policy language is available, add the follow-form, definition, and exclusion provisions that defeat UM/UIM coverage.

challenges.judge_assessment: The proposed distinction between permission to incorporate and actual incorporation has textual force if one considers only R.C. 3937.18(E), but it does not fairly account for the authorities quoted in the brief. Arn and St. Clair are presented as holding that the law effective on an actual renewal governs the scope of UM/UIM coverage, and Advent is cited for the same proposition where S.B. 267 predated the guarantee period. Because S.B. 97 removed a statutory obligation rather than adding contractual coverage, those authorities support Westport's position that the renewal was governed by the amended statute without proof of a separate endorsement. The stronger attack is the controlling-force problem posed by Storer, not the absence of an incorporation document.
challenges.suggested_response: Westport does not rely on a separate endorsement or written rejection to invoke S.B. 97. The relevant fact is that the policies renewed on January 1, 2002, after S.B. 97 became effective on October 31, 2001. Arn holds that at the time of renewal after S.B. 97 took effect, the insurer did not have to offer or include UM/UIM coverage, and such coverage could no longer be implied by operation of law. For that reason, the January 1, 2002 renewal was governed by S.B. 97.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not say S.B. 97 was 'incorporated into the policies' unless the record contains an endorsement or renewal document showing that. Reframe the point as a renewal-governs argument under Arn and St. Clair: the operative renewal occurred after S.B. 97 became effective, so the amended statute controlled without any separate offer/rejection form.

attacks_proposed.argument: Westport has not established the statutory delivery element merely by identifying its Kansas location and PS Management's Pennsylvania address. The brief states that the policies covered multiple named insureds, yet it identifies only one named insured's address and supplies no record evidence showing where the policies were delivered or issued for delivery to every relevant insured. Under Ohio's summary-judgment framework, the movant must point to evidence affirmatively demonstrating the absence of a genuine issue; the nonmovant's reciprocal burden arises only afterward.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without competent evidence conclusively establishing delivery outside Ohio, Westport has not negated an essential condition for application of R.C. 3937.18 and cannot obtain summary judgment on this ground.

attacks_proposed.argument: The declarations' listed garaging locations do not, without more, establish that no covered vehicle was registered or principally garaged in Ohio. The brief reports listed garaging locations in Florida and Pennsylvania and then asserts the broader conclusion that no vehicle was registered or principally garaged in Ohio, but no underlying registration records, complete policy schedules, or other evidentiary materials were supplied here. A summary-judgment movant must affirmatively demonstrate the absence of supporting evidence rather than rely on an unsupported conclusion.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the registration or principal-garaging issue remains unproven, Westport has not conclusively placed the Business Auto Policy outside R.C. 3937.18.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief does not independently establish the delivery and territorial facts for the Commercial Excess Policy. It acknowledges that the excess policy identifies no vehicles and can cover amounts above a retained limit where primary insurance is not afforded, but nevertheless treats it as territorially identical to the Business Auto Policy. That conclusion requires proof from the complete excess-policy language; it does not follow merely from identifying the auto policy as scheduled underlying insurance.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Failure to establish the excess policy's own scope, delivery, and relationship to covered automobile risks prevents summary judgment on the proposition that R.C. 3937.18 categorically does not apply to that policy.

Only after that showing does the reciprocal burden arise. judge_assessments.assessment: This lands as a substantial challenge to Westport's S.B. 97 alternative. Storer was precedent from this Court and stated a rule facially adverse to mid-guarantee-period incorporation. Decisions from other districts did not displace it, and the certified conflict confirms that the issue was unsettled rather than resolved in Westport's favor. Westport does offer a material distinction—S.B. 267 was effective before this guarantee period began—but whether that distinction avoids Storer is the disputed legal question. If the Court rejects the distinction, Westport loses the S.B. 97 ground, though it may still prevail on the independent territorial ground under R.C. 3937.18.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief acknowledges Storer, argues it involved guarantee periods that began before S.B. 267, cites Arn, Advent, St. Clair, and Shay, and discloses that the precise conflict was pending before the Ohio Supreme Court.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The controlling Ohio Supreme Court disposition of the certified Advent/Storer conflict, or any binding Eighth District treatment issued before decision here, would settle the point.

judge_assessments.assessment: This exposes a real gap in the categorical excess-policy argument. Westport describes the excess policy as covering not only amounts above primary insurance but also certain injuries above a retained limit when primary insurance is unavailable. On that description alone, absence of UM/UIM coverage in the underlying policies does not necessarily eliminate every route to excess coverage. Westport must rely on the excess policy's complete insuring agreement, definitions, exclusions, and follow-form provisions to show that the retained-limit feature does not reach the claimed automobile loss. Without that showing, the dependency rationale in u19 is insufficient. Westport could still prevail on the territorial or S.B. 97 grounds if either independently applies to the excess policy.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says the excess policy follows the underlying auto policy's terms for automobile liability and asserts that it need not provide UM/UIM coverage when the underlying policies do not, but it also states that the excess policy covers certain injuries above a retained limit when primary insurance is not afforded.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complete excess-policy insuring agreement, retained-limit provisions, automobile exclusions, and scheduled-underlying-insurance provisions would determine whether the apparent inconsistency is substantive.

judge_assessments.assessment: The general summary-judgment principle is sound, but the attack understates the record identified by the brief. Westport does not rely solely on its Kansas location and one address; it cites the policy exhibits and affirmatively states that both policies were delivered to the Pennsylvania named insured. The mere existence of additional named insureds does not establish that the policy had to be delivered separately to each one, and the attack cites no authority imposing that requirement. At most, opposing counsel could test whether the cited exhibits actually substantiate delivery in Pennsylvania; the proposed attack does not show a genuine dispute on the present record.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Units u40 and u59 state that the Business Auto and Commercial Excess policies were issued by Westport in Kansas to PS Management in Pennsylvania and delivered to the Pennsylvania named insured, with the policies themselves cited as exhibits.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Inspection of the declarations, delivery correspondence, and any policy-delivery affidavit would confirm whether the record supports Pennsylvania delivery.

judge_assessments.assessment: Policy declarations listing each covered auto and its garaging location are ordinary record evidence of principal garaging; the attack offers no authority requiring separate vehicle-registration records. More importantly, the statutory condition also requires delivery or issuance for delivery in Ohio, and Westport separately claims and supports delivery in Pennsylvania. Thus, even a marginal dispute about registration would not defeat this ground if out-of-state delivery is established. The generic summary-judgment citation does not make the declarations inadequate.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief cites Item Three of the Business Auto declarations, identifies all seven scheduled autos, and gives Florida or Pennsylvania as the garaging location for each. It separately asserts delivery in Pennsylvania.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complete declarations and vehicle schedule would settle whether every covered auto was listed and assigned an out-of-state garaging location.

judge_assessments.assessment: As framed, this misreads the brief. Westport expressly addresses the excess policy's delivery and says both policies were issued to and delivered to PS Management in Pennsylvania. It also cites policy language making the excess coverage subject to the underlying auto policy's terms and identifying that policy as scheduled primary insurance. Whether retained-limit coverage creates an independent automobile-coverage route is a legitimate issue, but that is captured by attack a8; it does not establish that the brief omitted the excess policy's delivery facts.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Unit u40 states that both policies were issued by Westport in Kansas to PS Management in Pennsylvania and that the excess policy follows the identified Business Auto Policy's terms, conditions, exclusions, definitions, and limitations for automobile liability.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complete excess policy would verify both its delivery information and the precise reach of its follow-form and retained-limit provisions.

judge_assessments.assessment: The proposed distinction between permission to incorporate and actual incorporation has textual force if one considers only R.C. 3937.18(E), but it does not fairly account for the authorities quoted in the brief. Arn and St. Clair are presented as holding that the law effective on an actual renewal governs the scope of UM/UIM coverage, and Advent is cited for the same proposition where S.B. 267 predated the guarantee period. Because S.B. 97 removed a statutory obligation rather than adding contractual coverage, those authorities support Westport's position that the renewal was governed by the amended statute without proof of a separate endorsement. The stronger attack is the controlling-force problem posed by Storer, not the absence of an incorporation document.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief quotes R.C. 3937.18(E) and relies on Arn, Advent, and St. Clair for the proposition that statutory changes may govern at a renewal within the guarantee period when S.B. 267 was already effective at the period's outset.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full opinions in Arn, Advent, and St. Clair would establish whether they required an express endorsement or treated renewal under the new law as sufficient.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited formulation requiring an actual renewal is relevant, but Westport points to interrogatory answers, policy dates, and separately issued annual policy documents identifying January 1, 2002 as a renewal. The initial one-month binder does not itself create a genuine dispute about whether the January 2002 transaction was a contractual renewal. Without contrary policy language or record evidence, the attack is speculative and the generic summary-judgment authority adds little.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that coverage was bound December 1, 2000, that policies were issued for January 1, 2001 and January 1, 2002, and that the January 1, 2002 policy was a renewal, citing interrogatory answers, an affidavit, and the policy exhibits.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The renewal clause, declarations, and January 2002 issuance documents would conclusively establish whether that transaction met the policy's contractual definition of renewal.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief already answers the nonproduction premise by stating that no physical December policy existed and that the binder and both later policies were produced. The attack does not identify a disputed binder provision that would change the statutory analysis. S.B. 267 was effective before coverage was first bound, and the accident occurred during the produced January 2002 policy. Binder terms could matter if plaintiffs showed that they altered the guarantee-period sequence or contained relevant UM/UIM coverage, but no such showing appears here. Nonproduction alone does not imply coverage.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Westport says the December binder was produced, no physical policy was printed for that month, the January 2001 and January 2002 policies were produced, and plaintiffs cited no law making nonproduction a basis for implied UM/UIM coverage.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The binder itself and the cited production notice would confirm its terms and eliminate any residual factual question about what was produced.

judge_assessments.assessment: The legal statement about the movant's initial burden is correct but does not identify a failure on this record. Westport points to policy declarations, schedules, interrogatory answers, an affidavit, and a production notice for the material propositions. Opposing counsel cannot convert disagreement with those materials into a Dresher violation merely by calling the propositions assertions. Any concrete deficiency must be tied to a particular exhibit or element, as in the retained-limit issue; the generalized procedural attack would not independently affect the judgment.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief supports its delivery, garaging, policy-period, renewal, and production assertions with identified policy exhibits, interrogatory answers, an affidavit, and a notice of compliance, then argues that plaintiffs supplied no contrary evidence.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review of the actual Civ.R. 56 materials would determine admissibility and whether each factual assertion is supported, but the proposed attack identifies no specific evidentiary defect.

judge_assessments.assessment: The inconsistent accident dates are an obvious drafting problem, but they are immaterial to the presented statutory issue because every stated date falls after the January 1, 2002 renewal and within the same January 2002–January 2003 policy period. The discrepancy would matter only if the precise date changed the governing policy or statutory version, which it does not on this record. A court would note the error but would not reverse summary judgment because of it.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief gives August 15, 2002 in u9, refers inconsistently to a July 2002 accident in u10, and uses July 15, 2002 in u90; all dates fall within the same annual policy period and after S.B. 97's effective date and the asserted renewal.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The accident report or complaint would establish the correct date, but the correction would not alter the renewal analysis unless it placed the loss in another policy period.

results.assessment: The brief has a workable structure and it does cite authorities for the renewal-based S.B. 97 theory, but as written it is not yet fully persuasive because the most serious obstacle is the intra-district conflict with Storer, which the brief can only distinguish, not neutralize. It also overstates the excess-policy point by treating lack of underlying UM/UIM coverage as categorically dispositive even though the policy description leaves another coverage route open. The incorporation issue is weaker than the Storer problem, but the brief still does not clearly show actual incorporation at renewal. The research leaves the territorial ground untested here, so that may remain a separate avenue of defense.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the central limitation on the lis-pendens assignment. R.C. 2703.26 and the authorities quoted by the brief protect whatever property right Solomon ultimately proves; they do not create that right or establish entitlement to specific performance. The brief separately argues that the extension remained effective and that Harwood anticipatorily breached, but those propositions remain disputed and depend heavily on the financing evidence. If Solomon cannot revive the underlying contract claim, Mustafa's notice of the litigation does not itself defeat Mustafa's title or possession.
challenges.suggested_response: Mustafa’s notice of Solomon’s claim did not itself create Solomon’s rights, and Solomon does not rely on notice for that proposition. The point is that Solomon’s contract rights were still being litigated when Harwood transferred title to Mustafa, and the record contains genuine disputes as to whether the December 6 extension was effective, whether Horvath’s December 13 termination was an anticipatory breach, and whether Solomon could have closed by December 14, 2007. Because the underlying right to specific performance remained unresolved, Mustafa took title subject to the outcome of that litigation, and summary judgment was improper.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Make clear that lis pendens does not itself prove Solomon’s rights, but that genuine disputes over the extension, termination, and financing left the underlying claim unresolved when Mustafa took title. The point is that summary judgment was improper because the predicate property claim was still in dispute.

challenges.opponent_argument: The lis-pendens theory confuses subordination with invalidity. The authorities quoted in the brief describe a pendente lite purchaser as taking subject to the eventual judgment; they do not make the deed void when executed. Ohio title principles likewise recognize that a deed passes title and that current record ownership may control present possession. Thus, Mustafa's acquisition remained effective unless and until Solomon actually prevailed on the underlying property claim.
challenges.why_it_matters: Timing and notice alone cannot justify declaring Mustafa's deed ineffective or reversing judgment without first establishing that Solomon had a superior substantive right to the property.

challenges.judge_assessment: The attack accurately identifies an overstatement in the requested remedy. The authorities the brief itself quotes say that a pendente lite purchaser takes subject to the eventual judgment, not that the conveyance is automatically void. Dickerson, Foundation Savings, and the quoted statutory language support subordination to a later adjudication in Solomon's favor. They do not support treating Mustafa's deed as void merely because it was executed during the action. The brief's reliance on Smith to call the deed fraudulent is not developed enough to bridge that gap. Solomon can still argue that the trial court improperly allowed Mustafa to use the deed to defeat a claim that had not been adjudicated, but he cannot obtain invalidation based on timing alone.
challenges.suggested_response: The authorities governing lis pendens do not render Mustafa’s deed void merely because it was executed while this action was pending. Rather, once Solomon filed suit, Mustafa took the property subject to the final adjudication of Solomon’s claims. R.C. 2703.26; Cook v. Mozer; Dickerson v. Curtin. The trial court therefore erred in treating Mustafa’s acquisition as defeating Solomon’s pending contract and specific-performance rights as a matter of law. If Solomon prevails on those claims, Mustafa’s deed and any interests derived from it cannot stand against that adjudication.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Revise the lis-pendens remedy language so it says Mustafa took subject to Solomon’s pending claim, not that the deed was automatically void or conveyed no rights. The argument should track the authorities the brief already quotes and reserve any stronger remedy for the point where Solomon actually prevails on the underlying property claim.

challenges.opponent_argument: Possession, improvements, and an unrecorded or escrowed deed do not by themselves establish occupying-claimant status. The statute as quoted in the brief requires that the claimant have obtained title and hold under a specified qualifying source. Although an Ohio deed need not be recorded to pass title, title still must actually pass; the brief merely says Harwood's deed remained deposited in escrow and labels Solomon an equitable owner without demonstrating completed delivery or another statutory category.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without proof that Solomon obtained and held qualifying title, he cannot invoke the occupying-claimant remedies merely because he occupied and improved the premises.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands squarely against the occupying-claimant theory. The statutory text quoted in the brief requires that the claimant have obtained title and hold under one of the specified sources. The record description says the deed remained in escrow and would be recorded only if Solomon timely paid the remaining amount. Calling Solomon an equitable owner or a contract purchaser does not, without more, show completed delivery of that deed or compliance with a statutory holding category. Possession and improvements satisfy other parts of the theory but cannot replace the title prerequisite. The cited title source only establishes that recording is not always necessary; it does not show that title passed under this conditional escrow.
challenges.suggested_response: The present record does not establish every statutory prerequisite for occupying-claimant status, because it does not show completed delivery of the deed or any other qualifying transfer of title. At most, the evidence of the executed escrow deed, Solomon’s possession, and the improvements he made raises a factual question that should not have been resolved against him on summary judgment. The trial court therefore erred in disposing of the occupying-claimant claim as a matter of law on this record.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Substantially narrow this assignment. The present record, as supplied, does not show completed delivery of the escrowed deed or another clearly qualifying transfer of title, so the brief should not claim Solomon proved occupying-claimant status as a matter of law.

challenges.opponent_argument: Unclean hands is an equitable consideration governing entitlement to equitable relief; it is not a blanket rule that prevents a party from obtaining summary judgment on every legal claim, defense, or counterclaim. The brief never identifies, defendant by defendant, which particular equitable remedy was barred or explains why the alleged conduct defeats the legal elements on which summary judgment rested.
challenges.why_it_matters: Even if some conduct could affect an equitable remedy such as specific performance or an injunction, that would not require wholesale reversal of every summary judgment entered for Harwood, Resource, and Horvath.

challenges.judge_assessment: The assignment treats unclean hands as a universal bar to summary judgment, which is too broad. The doctrine concerns a litigant's entitlement to equitable relief and requires a connection between the misconduct and the matter in which equity is invoked. The brief does not match the doctrine to each judgment, claim, counterclaim, or remedy. Even crediting the allegations of fraud and concealment, that would not automatically defeat summary judgment on legal claims or on claims failing for an independent element. The cited source is limited, but it at least confirms the doctrine's equitable setting; the more decisive problem is visible from the brief's requested wholesale remedy.
challenges.suggested_response: Unclean hands is an equitable doctrine, but here the conduct alleged against Harwood, Resource, and Horvath arose from the very transaction before the Court: the short-sale documents, the false HUD-1, the concealment of the Mustafa deal, and the premature termination of escrow. Those allegations go directly to the equitable relief and equitable enforcement appellees sought in this litigation, and the trial court could not grant such relief while the material facts remained disputed. At minimum, summary judgment on the equitable claims was improper.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Limit the unclean-hands argument to equitable relief and connect the alleged misconduct directly to the relief appellees sought. Do not present the doctrine as a blanket bar to every claim or judgment.

challenges.judge_assessment: The legal proposition is correct: a jury demand does not bar summary judgment, and R.C. 5303.11 refers to factual questions remaining after legal disposition. The brief's broad claim of an absolute jury right therefore cannot independently undo a properly supported summary judgment. But the attack does not fully dispose of the assignment because Solomon contends that damages and fee amounts involved unresolved facts and because his other assignments challenge the underlying liability rulings. If those rulings are reversed or the damages evidence was genuinely disputed, the jury issue may become material on remand.
challenges.suggested_response: Solomon does not contend that a jury demand, standing alone, prevented summary judgment. Rather, once genuine issues of material fact remained concerning Solomon’s ability to close, the amount of damages, and the amount and propriety of any fees, those issues had to be reserved for trial. R.C. 5303.11 requires a jury for a question of fact remaining undisposed of; it does not authorize the court to resolve disputed damages questions as a matter of law. Accordingly, to the extent the court disposed of damages issues that turned on disputed facts, Solomon was entitled to have those questions tried to a jury.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Delete the implication that the jury demand alone barred summary judgment. Recast the point as one about disputed damages questions that must be tried if liability is not resolved as a matter of law.

attacks_proposed.argument: The argument against RSB is entirely conditional: RSB's mortgages fail only if Mustafa lacked title. But the brief supplies no independent ground for invalidating RSB's interests and does not analyze RSB's own position. Because Ohio title principles recognize interests derived from the record owner, the derivative argument fails unless Solomon first overturns the judgment sustaining Mustafa's title.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Affirmance as to Mustafa independently requires affirmance as to RSB under the brief's own theory; the assignment adds no separate basis for reversal.

attacks_proposed.argument: Possession, improvements, and an unrecorded or escrowed deed do not by themselves establish occupying-claimant status. The statute as quoted in the brief requires that the claimant have obtained title and hold under a specified qualifying source. Although an Ohio deed need not be recorded to pass title, title still must actually pass; the brief merely says Harwood's deed remained deposited in escrow and labels Solomon an equitable owner without demonstrating completed delivery or another statutory category.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without proof that Solomon obtained and held qualifying title, he cannot invoke the occupying-claimant remedies merely because he occupied and improved the premises.

attacks_proposed.argument: The requested remedy also omits the statutory valuation and offset process. Ohio's occupying-claimant procedure calls for a jury only as to factual questions remaining for trial, and any amount for improvements is reduced by waste and the net value of rents and profits. The successful title claimant then receives statutory options concerning the land and improvements. The statute therefore does not authorize an automatic award of the improvements' asserted market value based solely on possession.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Even if Solomon qualified, the court could not simply order the compensation requested without resolving offsets, valuation, and the statutory post-verdict alternatives.

attacks_proposed.argument: A jury demand does not prevent disposition by summary judgment. R.C. 5303.11 requires a jury for a question of fact 'remaining undisposed of'; it does not create a jury issue after the court determines that no genuine factual dispute remains. The brief therefore cannot establish jury-trial error merely by showing that Solomon demanded a jury and that the court resolved liability or damages as a matter of law.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Unless Solomon first identifies a genuinely disputed, legally material damages fact, the jury demand supplies no independent ground for reversal.

attacks_proposed.argument: The assertion of an 'absolute' right to have a jury decide attorney fees is overbroad. Ohio's general rule is that attorney fees are unavailable absent statutory, contractual, or other recognized authorization. Whether such authorization exists is a threshold legal issue; only genuinely disputed factual questions remaining after that determination potentially require a jury. The brief does not separately analyze the legal basis for each fee award before declaring every aspect of the awards jury questions.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The existence of a jury demand cannot invalidate fee awards that turn on contractual or legal entitlement and undisputed evidence rather than unresolved factual questions.

attacks_proposed.argument: Unclean hands is an equitable consideration governing entitlement to equitable relief; it is not a blanket rule that prevents a party from obtaining summary judgment on every legal claim, defense, or counterclaim. The brief never identifies, defendant by defendant, which particular equitable remedy was barred or explains why the alleged conduct defeats the legal elements on which summary judgment rested.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Even if some conduct could affect an equitable remedy such as specific performance or an injunction, that would not require wholesale reversal of every summary judgment entered for Harwood, Resource, and Horvath.

attacks_proposed.argument: The assignment groups Resource with Harwood and Horvath, but the developed conclusion says only that Harwood and Horvath had unclean hands. The brief does not separately connect Resource's alleged HUD-1 conduct to a particular equitable claim Resource asserted or to the grounds on which Resource obtained summary judgment. Alleged wrongdoing toward WaMu does not, without that missing connection, establish that Resource was barred from judgment against Solomon.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The collective accusation cannot substitute for a defendant-specific showing, leaving no developed unclean-hands basis for reversing Resource's judgment.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the central limitation on the lis-pendens assignment. R.C. 2703.26 and the authorities quoted by the brief protect whatever property right Solomon ultimately proves; they do not create that right or establish entitlement to specific performance. The brief separately argues that the extension remained effective and that Harwood anticipatorily breached, but those propositions remain disputed and depend heavily on the financing evidence. If Solomon cannot revive the underlying contract claim, Mustafa's notice of the litigation does not itself defeat Mustafa's title or possession.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that the December 14 extension was effective, that the December 13 termination was an anticipatory breach, and that Gill's conflicting evidence creates a fact issue concerning Solomon's ability to close. It therefore does address the underlying merits, but not within the lis-pendens assignment and not conclusively.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The decisive research would be Ohio authority addressing whether lis pendens affords any relief after the plaintiff loses the underlying specific-performance or title claim.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack accurately identifies an overstatement in the requested remedy. The authorities the brief itself quotes say that a pendente lite purchaser takes subject to the eventual judgment, not that the conveyance is automatically void. Dickerson, Foundation Savings, and the quoted statutory language support subordination to a later adjudication in Solomon's favor. They do not support treating Mustafa's deed as void merely because it was executed during the action. The brief's reliance on Smith to call the deed fraudulent is not developed enough to bridge that gap. Solomon can still argue that the trial court improperly allowed Mustafa to use the deed to defeat a claim that had not been adjudicated, but he cannot obtain invalidation based on timing alone.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief repeatedly states that Mustafa could acquire no interest superior to Solomon and quotes authority that a purchaser takes subject to the final outcome. It also says the deed should be considered fraudulent and convey no rights, but it does not explain why the latter remedy follows before Solomon prevails on the underlying claim.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Reviewing Smith v. VanKirk and Ohio cases distinguishing a void deed from a valid conveyance subject to lis pendens would settle the precise remedial consequence.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands squarely against the occupying-claimant theory. The statutory text quoted in the brief requires that the claimant have obtained title and hold under one of the specified sources. The record description says the deed remained in escrow and would be recorded only if Solomon timely paid the remaining amount. Calling Solomon an equitable owner or a contract purchaser does not, without more, show completed delivery of that deed or compliance with a statutory holding category. Possession and improvements satisfy other parts of the theory but cannot replace the title prerequisite. The cited title source only establishes that recording is not always necessary; it does not show that title passed under this conditional escrow.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief relies on Solomon's possession, executory purchase agreements, and a deed deposited in escrow, characterizing those facts as color of title or equitable ownership. It does not analyze delivery of the deed, satisfaction of the escrow condition, or each statutory category in R.C. 5303.08.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Ohio decisions construing “obtained title” and the qualifying categories in R.C. 5303.08, particularly where a deed remains conditionally deposited in escrow, would be controlling.

judge_assessments.assessment: The assignment treats unclean hands as a universal bar to summary judgment, which is too broad. The doctrine concerns a litigant's entitlement to equitable relief and requires a connection between the misconduct and the matter in which equity is invoked. The brief does not match the doctrine to each judgment, claim, counterclaim, or remedy. Even crediting the allegations of fraud and concealment, that would not automatically defeat summary judgment on legal claims or on claims failing for an independent element. The cited source is limited, but it at least confirms the doctrine's equitable setting; the more decisive problem is visible from the brief's requested wholesale remedy.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief cites Seitz, lists alleged misconduct, and concludes that summary judgment should have been denied. It does not identify the particular equitable relief sought by each appellee or explain how unclean hands negates each independent legal ground for judgment.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full text of Seitz and controlling Ohio Supreme Court authority on whether unclean hands can defeat legal claims or merely equitable remedies would sharpen the scope.

judge_assessments.assessment: The legal proposition is correct: a jury demand does not bar summary judgment, and R.C. 5303.11 refers to factual questions remaining after legal disposition. The brief's broad claim of an absolute jury right therefore cannot independently undo a properly supported summary judgment. But the attack does not fully dispose of the assignment because Solomon contends that damages and fee amounts involved unresolved facts and because his other assignments challenge the underlying liability rulings. If those rulings are reversed or the damages evidence was genuinely disputed, the jury issue may become material on remand.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Solomon demanded a jury, cites authority that damages are generally for the jury, and argues that attorney fees sought as compensatory damages had to be submitted to a jury. It does not acknowledge that summary judgment remains available when no genuine issue of material fact exists.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The summary-judgment motions and supporting damages evidence would show whether any amount or causation issue was genuinely disputed rather than merely subject to a jury demand.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a substantial defendant-specific defect, although the attack slightly overstates the absence of allegations against Resource. The brief does accuse Resource of preparing the HUD-1, certifying it to WaMu, using Solomon's funds, and prematurely terminating escrow. But the unclean-hands section's conclusion expressly addresses only Harwood and Horvath, and it never identifies equitable relief Resource sought or explains how the alleged wrong to WaMu defeats the grounds for Resource's summary judgment and counterclaim. The separate fiduciary-duty section may support substantive claims against Resource, but it does not cure the remedial gap in the unclean-hands assignment.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief includes Resource in the assignment heading and in the allegation concerning the HUD-1, then concludes only that Harwood and Horvath came to court with unclean hands. Its later Resource section separately argues fiduciary duty, contract, and negligence.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The trial court's stated grounds for Resource's judgment and the nature of Resource's counterclaim relief would determine whether unclean hands could affect any part of that judgment.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack correctly characterizes the RSB assignment as wholly derivative. The brief provides no independent argument concerning RSB's notice, priority, defenses, or mortgage status. Consequently, affirmance of Mustafa's title defeats the RSB assignment under Solomon's own framing. If Solomon succeeds in showing that his property interest has priority under lis pendens, however, the derivative nature of RSB's mortgages may be enough to require reconsideration; the absence of a separate theory is not necessarily fatal at that point. This assignment therefore adds no independent route to reversal but can follow a successful title ruling.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states only that RSB holds two mortgages, that all of its rights derive from Mustafa, and that the arguments against Mustafa apply equally to RSB.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: RSB's mortgage dates, the title commitment exclusions, and any asserted bona-fide-mortgagee or priority defense would determine whether its interests are entirely derivative in the manner the brief assumes.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited statutes do establish a valuation, offset, jury, and post-verdict procedure, but the attack goes beyond what the brief requests. Solomon principally asks that the Occupying Claimant Law be applied and that the improvement claim be adjudicated before eviction; he does not ask the appellate court to calculate and immediately award an unreduced amount. The statutory procedure would govern on remand if he first proves qualifying claimant status. Failure to detail every valuation step does not defeat the threshold applicability argument, although the brief's reference to the fair market value of all improvements is imprecise.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief quotes R.C. 5303.08, asserts entitlement to compensation for lasting improvements before dispossession, and relies on Platt for pre-eviction adjudication. It does not discuss offsets or the later procedural provisions.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: No further research is necessary unless Solomon seeks a specific appellate award rather than remand for statutory proceedings.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited general rule governing when attorney fees are recoverable does not answer who decides fees that are themselves claimed as compensatory contract damages. The brief specifically cites Stonehenge and Keal for jury determination in that setting. The attack is correct that legal entitlement must first exist and that summary judgment remains possible on undisputed facts, but it does not confront the brief's more specific authorities or show that the awards here were conventional court-awarded fees rather than damages. On the present sources, this does not materially undermine the assignment beyond the procedural point already captured by attack a6.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief expressly characterizes Harwood's and Resource's requested fees as compensatory damages and cites Stonehenge and Keal for submitting such damages to a jury.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The fee provisions, counterclaim theories, and full holdings of Stonehenge and Keal would determine whether these fees were damages for a jury or collateral fee awards for the court.

results.verdict: partly persuasive, but still exposed on several central reme
results.assessment: The brief has its strongest footing where it argues that lis pendens subordinates Mustafa’s deed rather than voiding it outright, and where it ties the occupying-claimant and RSB issues to disputed title and possession. But it remains vulnerable on the biggest points: it does not yet supply the title prerequisite for occupying-claimant relief, it overreaches by treating unclean hands as a blanket bar to summary judgment, and it frames the lis-pendens issue too broadly by relying on notice alone. The jury-demand argument is also incomplete because a jury demand does not itself block summary judgment. The research leaves the core factual disputes unresolved, especially the contract-extension and closing issues.

challenges.opponent_argument: The lis-pendens argument confuses taking title subject to pending litigation with receiving no title at all. The authority quoted in the brief itself states that a third-party purchaser takes subject to the final outcome; it does not establish that the intervening deed is automatically void before that outcome. Retrieved Ohio authority likewise describes a third-party purchaser as taking subject to the vendee’s rights, while recognizing that present possession may depend on existing record title. [Sources 22, 24] Mustafa’s notice therefore may prevent him from defeating any rights Solomon ultimately proves, but notice does not itself establish those rights or invalidate the deed.
challenges.why_it_matters: Lis pendens cannot independently establish Solomon’s title, specific-performance entitlement, or present right to possession. If Solomon’s underlying contract claim fails, the doctrine provides no superior interest to enforce against Mustafa.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the principal legal defect in the lis-pendens assignment. R.C. 2703.26 and the authorities quoted in the brief make a pendente lite transferee subject to the eventual judgment; they do not automatically void the transfer or establish the plaintiff's underlying property rights. Sources 22 and 24 are consistent with that distinction. Mustafa's actual notice strengthens the binding effect of any eventual judgment for Solomon but does not itself establish specific performance or a present right to possession. The court could therefore reject the requested treatment of the deed as fraudulent or void while preserving only the narrower proposition that Mustafa is bound by the outcome of Solomon's viable property claims.
challenges.suggested_response: The doctrine of lis pendens does not mean that Mustafa’s deed is void ab initio. It means that, because Solomon’s action was already pending and Mustafa had actual notice of Solomon’s claim, Mustafa took title subject to the final adjudication of Solomon’s rights. Accordingly, if Solomon prevails on his contract and specific-performance claims, Mustafa cannot use his later-acquired deed to defeat those rights or to evict Solomon free of the court’s judgment.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the lis-pendens point. The brief should stop saying the deed was automatically void or conveyed no rights, and instead argue only that Mustafa took subject to whatever rights Solomon ultimately proves in the pending specific-performance action.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief’s own account does not show that Solomon could close by the asserted deadline. It concedes that Gill lacked a loan application, financial statements, tax returns, credit and capacity information, a legal opinion concerning the federal tax lien, and agreed loan terms; Gill’s notes stated that he needed an extension to decide whether to commit and later stated he could not resolve the issues within twenty-four hours. The affidavit was also expressly conditional—financing would proceed only “when all loan conditions were met.” A possibility that unresolved conditions might have been satisfied is not a specific fact showing that financing would be available by 4:00 p.m. December 14. [Source 11]
challenges.why_it_matters: The alleged credibility disputes do not cure the absence of evidence that the conditions would actually be satisfied by the deadline. Without timely financing, Solomon cannot show that the asserted early termination caused the failed closing or deprived him of a transaction he could complete.

challenges.judge_assessment: The financing record is materially weaker than the brief's rhetoric suggests. Gill identified numerous unresolved underwriting matters and stated that he had not made a final commitment. That creates a substantial causation and readiness problem. But the attack cannot fairly say there was no contrary Civ.R. 56 evidence: Gill's earlier affidavit expressly stated that he was willing and able to finance approximately $320,000 and that the money was available to close before the deadline. Because the affidavit preceded the adverse deposition testimony, the record presents a genuine contradiction rather than an obvious post-deposition sham. Those facts permit a jury to conclude that Horvath acted with conscious disregard of Solomon’s rights, which satisfies the malice exception recognized in Scholler.

The brief has substantial authority that attorney fees sought as compensatory damages are jury issues, but it does not identify record evidence disputing the amount, reasonableness, necessity, or causal attribution of the particular awards. Thus, the broad assertion that all damages had to go to a jury is insufficient by itself. The assignment remains stronger if the underlying liability judgments are reversed or if the damages submissions reveal genuine factual disputes.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief cites constitutional and Ohio authority stating that damages, including attorney fees claimed as compensatory damages, are for a jury, and notes that Solomon filed a jury demand. It does not identify specific evidentiary disputes concerning each damages award.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The damages motions, supporting billing records or affidavits, Solomon's oppositions, and the full Stonehenge and Keal opinions would show whether any award remained genuinely disputed and whether those cases preclude summary judgment on undisputed fee damages.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands well as to tortious interference. The brief's lis-pendens discussion does not supply the elements of interference, and notice of a competing contract plus acquisition of title does not by itself establish intentional procurement of breach, lack of justification, causation, and damages. Source 11 supports the need for specific Civ.R. 56 facts, although it does not itself supply the substantive tort elements. On the appellate presentation provided, the court could treat the interference theory as undeveloped and decline to use it as an independent ground for reversal.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The assignment heading alleges interference, and the factual narrative describes Mustafa's knowledge, his competing purchase, and the eviction plan. The argument section then develops lis pendens but does not separately state or apply the elements of tortious interference.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Controlling Ohio tortious-interference authority and the precise claims adjudicated in Mustafa's summary-judgment order would confirm whether the omission constitutes forfeiture under the appellate briefing rules.

judge_assessments.assessment: The privity branch is vulnerable. A contract with the lawyer's client does not automatically create the required privity, and Macken's shared objective is not obviously comparable to an arm's-length buyer and seller whose interests became adverse. But the attack understates the alternative malice showing. The brief does more than cite complaint allegations: it identifies evidence that Horvath allegedly confirmed the extension, executed the Mustafa contract, concealed that transaction, and attempted termination before the stated deadline. If those facts are supported by Civ.R. 56 materials, a court cannot reject them merely because the expert opinion assumes their truth. Source 11 supports only the evidentiary burden, not the substantive conclusion that neither Scholler exception is met. The advocate risks losing the privity theory but may preserve the claim through malice.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief asserts privity through the Harwood-Solomon contract and concurrent interest in completing the sale. Separately, it identifies Horvath's alleged concealment, competing contract, and attempted termination as conscious disregard, cites Davis for treating malice ordinarily as a factual issue, and references expert testimony conditioned on the alleged facts.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full Scholler, Macken, and Davis opinions are needed to determine the exact meaning of privity, concurrency, and malicious conduct for nonclient attorney liability.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack identifies a real underdevelopment but overstates the absence of any operative direction. The brief points to the purchase addendum, the asserted December 14 extension, Resource's knowledge of that extension, and Resource's return of funds at 2:00 p.m. as the instructions and conduct at issue. Those facts could support a breach if the governing escrow documents required Resource to continue holding the funds. Still, the brief does not quote or systematically apply the complete escrow instructions, and it does not separately trace causation and damages for contract, fiduciary-duty, and negligence theories. Source 59 supports the need for injury and causation in negligence but not the broader escrow-contract proposition. The larger appellate risk is that the assignment challenges an indemnification provision while the argument scarcely analyzes that provision.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief cites authority defining an escrow agent's fiduciary and contractual duties, alleges a false HUD-1, use of Solomon's funds, partiality toward Harwood, and termination at 2:00 p.m. despite an extension through the close of business, and asserts that the same facts support negligence.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complete escrow agreement, standard conditions, indemnity clause, written instructions, and evidence of the loss attributed to Resource are necessary to determine whether a triable breach exists and whether indemnification applies.

judge_assessments.assessment: Source 11 supports the general Civ.R. 56 requirement of specific evidence, but the proposed attack inaccurately portrays the brief as relying only on accusations. The brief cites deposition testimony, the HUD-1, the WaMu stipulation sheet, transaction documents, communications, and alleged contract alteration. Whether those materials are admissible and prove inequitable conduct cannot be resolved from the attack's generic citation. The voicemail alone is plainly equivocal, and the brief does fail to explain how unclean hands affects each judgment, particularly legal claims or relief sought by parties other than Harwood and Horvath. That narrower, claim-specific objection is substantial, but the proposed wholesale factual-support attack overreaches and lacks substantive unclean-hands authority.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief relies on the voicemail together with the HUD-1, short-payoff documents, IOLTA transfer, alleged concealment and contract alteration, the Mustafa transfer, and the eviction proceedings. It concludes collectively that these acts constitute unclean hands but does not apply the doctrine separately to each claim or form of relief.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Seitz and controlling Ohio authority on the direct-connection requirement, application to legal versus equitable relief, and use of unclean hands against counterclaims would permit a properly focused attack.

judge_assessments.assessment: The retrieved authorities do not adequately support this attack. Sources 40 and 44 concern oral land agreements or rental-agreement modifications, while the asserted extension here was contained in a writing sent by Harwood's representative. The brief's theory is that Solomon accepted that written offer orally and that Horvath then acted consistently with the extension by informing Resource of the December 14 deadline. The fact that Solomon did not return his signed copy may matter under ordinary formation rules or any express acceptance requirement, but the attack has not shown that the statute of frauds invalidates a writing signed or sent by the party to be charged. It also overlooks the brief's reliance on Horvath's communication to Resource as conduct recognizing the extension.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that the letter did not require return by facsimile, that Lynch orally communicated Solomon's acceptance, that the extension fee was payable at closing, and that Horvath confirmed the December 14 deadline to Resource.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The extension letter, its signature and delivery history, the original contract's modification clause, and Ohio authority on acceptance of a written real-estate modification would resolve formation.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief itself presents the RSB assignment as entirely derivative, so the attack largely restates rather than defeats it. Lis pendens would not automatically void the mortgages, but if Solomon ultimately established a property interest superior to Mustafa's pendente lite interest, RSB's later mortgages could be subject to that adjudication. Conversely, if Mustafa's judgment stands, the RSB assignment necessarily fails. The court would reach RSB only after resolving the underlying property claims; there is no independent issue on the argument presented.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief expressly says RSB's rights derive from Mustafa and that the same arguments apply to RSB if Mustafa did not receive good title.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The mortgage dates, RSB's notice, and the precise relief sought against the mortgages would matter only if Solomon first establishes a superior property interest.

results.assessment: The brief has real force where it points to conflicting financing evidence and a jury-triable factual dispute, and the malice theory against Horvath is not wholly unsupported. But it is weakest where it treats lis pendens as if it voided Mustafa’s deed, when the challenged doctrine only makes him take subject to the outcome, not defeat title outright. The occupying-claimant argument is also underdeveloped because the brief does not show that Solomon satisfied the statute’s title and holding requirements. The interference and escrow theories likewise need tighter element-by-element support and clearer record citations; as written, those parts read more like conclusions than Civ.R. 56 proof.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the most consequential attack. Even if Appellee knowingly acquiesced in the assignment and thereby lost the right to object to Wilson's occupancy, the brief does not establish that Carano and TSC were released from their contractual obligations. Waiver of a forfeiture or possessory remedy is not necessarily a novation, release, or discharge of the original lessee. Sources 3 and 24 support a distinction between possession and contract damages, although they arise in eviction settings and do not directly decide an original commercial tenant's liability after assignment. The gap matters because the appealed judgment is monetary. Unless the lease, the assignment, or applicable Ohio law makes Appellee's consent discharge the assignors, the waiver theory does not by itself defeat the damages award.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee’s acquiescence to Wilson’s possession and receipt of rent from Wilson or his corporation at minimum creates a factual dispute whether Appellants remained liable for the rent Appellee now seeks. The judgment entered below is a money judgment, and Appellee was not entitled to summary judgment on that claim while the evidence permitted a finding that Appellee had accepted the assignee as the party paying rent and had acquiesced in the post-assignment arrangement. At minimum, the case should be remanded for determination of the proper obligor and amount owed, if any.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not claim that waiver of the assignment objection automatically erased the monetary judgment. Either add authority or a record basis for discharge, or narrow the request for relief to the disputed amount and the identity of the obligor on the rent claim.
